targetWord.definition: very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or less powerful person

etymology.narrative: From Latin magnanimis (great-souled), from magnus (great) + animus (soul).

exampleSentences: The magnanimous victor showed mercy to the defeated.
It was magnanimous of her to forgive such a betrayal.

clues.text: This word shares its root with "magnanimity" and "magnificent".
Sometimes described as "benevolent", this adjective describes a particular quality.
Often used to describe positive moral qualities

tossups.explanation:
MAGNANIMOUS (/mæɡˈnænɪməs/)

Definition: very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or less powerful person

Etymology: From Latin magnanimis (great-souled), from magnus (great) + animus (soul).

Example: "The magnanimous victor showed mercy to the defeated."

Memory tip: MAGNA-NIMOUS = having a GREAT (magnus) SOUL (animus)

targetWord.definition: excessively unwilling to spend money or use resources; stingy

etymology.narrative: From Latin parsimonia (frugality, thrift), from parcere (to spare, be sparing).

exampleSentences: The parsimonious millionaire refused to tip.
His parsimonious habits extended to turning off all lights.

targetWord.definition: diligent and attentive; very careful about doing what is right

etymology.narrative: From Latin scrupulosus (anxious, cautious), from scrupulus (small sharp stone). Like a pebble in the shoe causing discomfort.

exampleSentences: The scrupulous accountant checked every figure twice.
She was scrupulous about following ethical guidelines.
targetWord.mnemonic: SCRUP-ulous = careful like a pebble (scrupulus) in your shoe makes you careful where you step

etymology.narrative: From Middle English cravant, from Old French cravante (defeated), past participle of cravanter (to crush, defeat).

exampleSentences: The craven soldier fled before the battle even began.
His craven surrender without a fight shamed his family.
targetWord.mnemonic: CRAVEN sounds like "cave in" - a craven person caves in under pressure

CRAVEN (/ˈkreɪvən/)

Definition: contemptibly lacking in courage; cowardly

Etymology: From Middle English cravant, from Old French cravante (defeated), past participle of cravanter (to crush, defeat).
